beats.text: A sequence lists individual terms in an indexed order. Here the terms are one half, one fourth, one eighth, and so on, with each term half the previous one. Their values approach zero as the index grows.

A series instead adds terms, and its partial sums form another sequence. The first sums are one half, three fourths, and seven eighths. Those sums increase even while the individual terms decrease, because each newly added term is positive.

The gap from the partial sum to one halves each time. After n terms that gap is one over two to the n, giving this exact finite-sum formula. Since the gap approaches zero, the infinite geometric series converges to one.

The harmonic terms also approach zero, but their sum diverges. Four terms from one fifth through one eighth each exceed or equal one eighth, totaling at least one half. Every doubled block repeats this lower bound, forcing unbounded partial sums.

practice.prompt: List the first four terms of a_n=2/3ⁿ for n starting at one.
Find the sum 1/3+1/9+1/27+… and state why it converges.
practice.answer: It is geometric with first term1/3 and ratio1/3, so the sum is(1/3)/(1−1/3)=1/2 because the ratio magnitude is below one.

practice.prompt: A sequence of terms tends to zero. Does this alone prove their infinite series converges? Explain with a counterexample.
practice.answer: No. Terms1/n tend to zero, but the harmonic series diverges; grouped blocks keep adding at least a fixed positive amount.

takeaway: Terms and partial sums are different sequences; vanishing terms alone do not ensure a finite sum.
scope: Sequence limits, geometric partial sums, and a divergence counterexample.
title: Sequences and series
objective: Reason about limiting terms, partial sums, and convergence of basic models.
